title: The Office Firm That Burned $47 Billion
hook: A firm that rented out desks and chairs was once worth $47 billion -- more than Ford or GM. Then it tried to sell shares to the public, and in six weeks lost $38 billion of that worth without selling a single one.
body:
WeWork Inc. was a coworking real-estate company built by Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey, founded in 2010 out of a single floor in Manhattan's SoHo. It grew from a $1.4 billion valuation in 2014 to $10.5 billion by 2016, after SoftBank's Masayoshi Son committed $4.4 billion in 2017. By January 2019 a new funding round valued the renamed 'The We Company' at $47 billion -- more than Ford or General Motors, despite owning almost none of the real estate it operated. On August 14, 2019, the firm filed an S-1 registration statement ahead of a planned IPO. The filing disclosed a $1.93 billion net loss on $1.82 billion of 2018 revenue, a non-GAAP metric called 'Community Adjusted EBITDA,' a $5.9 million trademark payment to a firm Neumann controlled, and Founder shares carrying 20 votes each. Within days, investors and reporters picked the filing apart, and backers cut their price guesses by more than half. Neumann resigned as CEO on September 24, 2019; the company withdrew its IPO filing on September 30. SoftBank stepped in with a rescue package worth roughly $9.5 billion, while Neumann exited with a package worth up to $1.7 billion. That November, WeWork laid off 2,400 workers. By May 2020, Son told investors on an earnings call, 'I was wrong,' as SoftBank marked its stake down to $2.9 billion. WeWork went public a second way, via a SPAC merger with BowX Acquisition Corp., beginning to trade on the NYSE on October 21, 2021, at a $9 billion valuation. In August 2022, Andreessen Horowitz invested $350 million in Neumann's next company, Flow, valuing it at $1 billion before it had opened a single building. WeWork issued a 'going concern' warning in August 2023, and on November 6, 2023, WeWork and 517 affiliated entities filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, listing $18.6 billion in debt against $15 billion in assets. Neumann, backed by Flow, bid roughly $500 million to buy WeWork back in March 2024, then abandoned the bid that spring. WeWork emerged from bankruptcy as a private company on June 11, 2024, having eliminated more than $4 billion of debt. No named person in this story was criminally charged, convicted, or sentenced -- this is a governance and hubris story, not a fraud prosecution. This is what SEC filings, WeWork's own S-1, and contemporaneous CNBC, Fortune, TechCrunch and PYMNTS reporting say happened.
